# sysutils_swap (Resource)

Manages a swap area: a swap file that the provider allocates, or an existing block device such as a partition. Formats it with `mkswap(8)`, enables it with `swapon(8)` and, optionally, adds it to `/etc/fstab` so that it is enabled at boot. On destroy the swap area is disabled with `swapoff(8)`, its `/etc/fstab` entry is removed and a swap file the provider created is deleted. Requires root privileges.

A `path` starting with `/dev/` names an existing block device, which is used whole; any other path is a swap file of `size_mib` MiB that the provider creates if it is missing.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# A 2 GiB swap file, enabled now and at boot.
resource "sysutils_swap" "file" {
  path     = "/swapfile"
  size_mib = 2048
}

# A swap partition, preferred over the swap file. The partition must be
# blank or already formatted as swap; set force = true to format a
# partition that still holds a file system.
resource "sysutils_swap" "partition" {
  path     = "/dev/disk/by-partuuid/0f3c7a1e-02"
  priority = 10
}

# A swap file for an image being built below root_dir: created and added
# to the image's /etc/fstab, but not enabled on the build host.
provider "sysutils" {
  alias    = "image"
  root_dir = "/srv/images/web/rootfs"
}

resource "sysutils_swap" "image" {
  provider = sysutils.image
  path     = "/swapfile"
  size_mib = 512
  enabled  = false
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `path` (String) Absolute path of the swap file, or of an existing block device if it starts with `/dev/`, such as `"/dev/sdb2"` or `"/dev/disk/by-uuid/..."`. The parent directory of a swap file must exist, and it and every directory above it must belong to root and not be writable by other users (sticky directories such as `/tmp` excepted); the file itself must not be a symlink. Must be in canonical form (no `.`/`..` segments, duplicate or trailing slashes). Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `enabled` (Boolean) Whether the swap area is in use now. If `false`, it is disabled with `swapoff` but kept, and with `persist = true` still enabled at boot. Must be `false` with the provider's `root_dir`, which prepares a swap file and its `/etc/fstab` entry inside the tree without enabling it. Defaults to `true`.
- `force` (Boolean) Allow overwriting data. Without it, the provider refuses to run `mkswap` on a block device that holds a file system, volume or partition table signature, to enable a block device whose swap header shares it with such a signature, and to format, resize or replace an existing file it did not create. An existing swap file that other users may have opened, because it belongs to one of them or its mode grants group or other users access, is never enabled as it is: with `force`, or if the provider created it, it is replaced by a new file. Other swap areas that are already formatted are used as they are either way. Defaults to `false`.
- `persist` (Boolean) Whether the swap area has an entry in `/etc/fstab` (inside `root_dir`, if set), so that it is enabled at boot. If `true`, the entry `<path> none swap sw[,pri=<priority>] 0 0` is added or updated; if `false`, any swap entry for `path` is removed. Defaults to `true`.
- `priority` (Number) Priority of the swap area, between 0 and 32767, as in `swapon -p`. Areas with higher priority are used first; areas with the same priority are used in turn. Written to `/etc/fstab` as the `pri=` option. If not set, the kernel assigns a negative priority below all others and it is not managed.
- `size_mib` (Number) Size of the swap file in MiB, between 1 and 8388608 (8 TiB). Required for swap files, and must not be set for block devices, which are used whole. Changing it disables the swap file, replaces it with one of the new size and enables that. Reads as `0` if the file is missing or no longer holds a swap area.

### Read-Only

- `created` (Boolean) Whether the provider created the swap file, in which case destroying the resource deletes it. `false` for block devices and for swap files that existed before, which are kept on destroy.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `path`).
- `uuid` (String) UUID of the swap area, as written by `mkswap`; empty if it has none. It changes whenever the provider formats the swap area again.

## Behavior

### Create

1. The provider refuses to create the resource if `path` is already an active swap area or `/etc/fstab` already has a swap entry for it. Destroying the resource would disable that swap area or remove that entry, so import it instead.
2. The swap area is prepared:
   - **Missing swap file:** a new file is created under a temporary name next to `path` with mode `0600`, owned by root, allocated with `fallocate(2)` (on file systems without it, zeros are written, like `dd if=/dev/zero`), formatted with `mkswap`, and renamed to `path`. A failure leaves nothing behind. On btrfs, copy-on-write is turned off for the file (`chattr +C`) first, as swap files require. `created` is `true`, so the file is deleted on destroy.
   - **Existing swap file:** a file that already holds a swap area of exactly `size_mib` is used as it is, without `mkswap`, provided no other user could have opened it: it must belong to root and its mode must grant group and other users no access. Its mode is then set to `0600` and its group to root. A file that belongs to another user or has a mode such as `0644` is refused, because changing its mode or owner does not revoke a descriptor opened before, through which swapped-out memory could be read or modified. Any other existing file is refused as well, because `mkswap` would destroy its contents. In both cases, `force = true` replaces the file with a new swap file. Either way `created` is `false`, and the file is kept on destroy.
   - **Directory checks:** `mkswap` and `swapon` take a path and follow symlinks, so the directory of a swap file, every directory above it and every directory reached through a symlink on the way must belong to root and not be writable by other users. Sticky directories such as `/tmp` are allowed, as long as the entries below them that the path passes through belong to root.
   - **Block device:** a device that already holds a swap area is used as it is, unless it is not active and also holds a file system, volume or partition table signature, as happens when a file system is created over an old swap area without wiping it; `swapon` would overwrite that data, so such a device is refused unless `force = true` is set. Otherwise, `mkswap` runs only if the device holds no file system, volume or partition table signature. The provider checks for the most common signatures itself and then asks `blkid -p`, if it is installed, which knows many more. With `force = true`, `mkswap -f` formats the device anyway. A device that is mounted, part of a device-mapper, LVM or RAID volume, or otherwise opened exclusively is refused even with `force`.
3. If `enabled` is `true`, the swap area is enabled with `swapon [-p <priority>] -- <path>`.
4. If `persist` is `true`, the line `<path> none swap sw[,pri=<priority>] 0 0` is appended to `/etc/fstab`.

Enabling comes first, so a swap area the kernel refuses (for example, a swap file on a file system without swap support) fails the apply before it is written to `/etc/fstab`. Afterwards, the provider checks `/proc/swaps` to confirm that the swap area is active with the configured priority.

### Update

- A changed `size_mib` disables the swap file, replaces it with a new, formatted one of the new size and enables that again. A swap file the provider did not create is only replaced with `force = true`.
- A swap file whose owner or mode was changed so that other users could open it reads as having an empty `uuid`, and the next apply replaces it with a new file, subject to the same rule.
- A changed `priority` of an active swap area disables it and enables it again, since the kernel cannot change the priority of an active swap area. The `/etc/fstab` entry is updated.
- `enabled = false` runs `swapoff` and `enabled = true` runs `swapon`.
- `persist = false` removes the `/etc/fstab` entry and `persist = true` adds it.
- Changing `path` replaces the resource.

`swapoff` has to move every page in the swap area back into memory. It fails if there is not enough free memory, and it can take a while on a busy host.

### Destroy

The swap area is disabled with `swapoff`, its `/etc/fstab` entry is removed, and the swap file is deleted if `created` is `true`. Block devices, and swap files that existed before or were imported, are kept. If `swapoff` fails, the destroy fails and the `/etc/fstab` entry and the file are kept.

## Editing /etc/fstab

`/etc/fstab` is edited like for [`sysutils_mount`](./mount.md): atomically, keeping the file's mode, owner, ACLs and SELinux label, all comments and every other entry, including other swap entries. An entry belongs to the resource when its third field is `swap` and its first field is `path`; entries naming the same swap area in another way, for example as `UUID=...`, are not recognised. If there are several entries for `path`, the next apply that changes the resource removes all but one.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the swap file or device, `/proc/swaps` and `/etc/fstab`:

- `enabled` is `true` if `/proc/swaps` lists the swap area. If it was disabled, the plan shows `enabled` changing to `true`.
- `size_mib` is the size of the swap area in the swap file's header, or of the file if they differ, or of the active swap area in `/proc/swaps` if that differs from the file by more than 1 MiB. It reads as `0` if the file is missing or no longer holds a swap area; the next apply then creates or formats it again (a file that the provider did not create only with `force = true`). A size that is not a whole number of MiB is rounded away from the configured size, so it always shows up as a diff.
- `uuid` is read from the swap header, and is empty if there is none. When the plan may format the swap area again, `uuid` and `created` are shown as known after apply.
- `persist` is `true` if `/etc/fstab` has a swap entry for `path`.
- `priority` is read from the `pri=` option of the `/etc/fstab` entry and from `/proc/swaps`. A missing, added or different `pri=` option shows up as a diff, and so does an active swap area whose priority differs from the configured one, for example after `swapon` without `-p`. If `priority` is not set, the priority the kernel assigns is not compared.

## Import

An existing swap file or device can be imported by its path:

```shell
# By the path of the swap file or block device. /etc/fstab and /proc/swaps
# provide the other settings. Imported swap files are kept on destroy.
terraform import sysutils_swap.file /swapfile
```

`enabled`, `persist` and `priority` come from `/proc/swaps` and `/etc/fstab`, and `size_mib` from the file. `created` is `false`, so an imported swap file is never deleted on destroy. The import fails if the path does not exist, is not an active swap area and has no swap entry in `/etc/fstab`.

## Root Directory

With the provider's [`root_dir`](../index.md#root-directory), `path` is a swap file inside the tree and `/etc/fstab` is the tree's own. This prepares a swap file for an image: the file is created, formatted and added to the tree's `/etc/fstab`. `enabled` must be `false`, because `swapon` would enable swap on the host building the image; block devices are refused for the same reason.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root.
- Swap files need a file system with swap support: ext4, XFS and btrfs work; tmpfs, overlayfs (the root file system of most containers) and network file systems don't. In containers, `swapon` is usually not permitted at all.
- A new swap file must be in a directory owned by root that other users cannot write to, unless it has the sticky bit set like `/tmp`. `mkswap` and `swapon` follow symlinks, so another user who could replace the file with a symlink could make them overwrite any file.
- `mkswap`, `swapon` and `swapoff` are each limited to 30 minutes.
- systemd creates `.swap` units from `/etc/fstab` at boot and on `systemctl daemon-reload`, which the provider does not run. You can run it with [`sysutils_exec`](./exec.md) using `triggers`.
- The provider [serialises](../index.md#concurrency-and-locking) its own edits of `/etc/fstab`, but does not lock the file against other tools. A concurrent edit by another tool is detected and fails the apply instead of being overwritten.
